role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: The one-page memo: a decision on a single sheet
summary: A one-page memo forces you to decide what matters before anyone else reads it. This lesson gives the six-part structure of a decision memo, shows how to cut a long draft to one page, and explains why the strongest sentence in professional life is a promise to confirm by a date rather than a guess.
body:
Mr Shabazz, if you cannot put a decision on one page, you have not finished thinking about it. The page is not a summary of your work. It is the test of whether the work is done.

Recall

Q. Can a quick email reply bind you to a price?

A. Often it can. Many courts judge agreement by what a reasonable reader would conclude, so a reply that reads as acceptance may be treated as one, depending on the contract and the law.

Q. What two forces set your alertness at any hour?

A. The body clock, with its low in the small hours, and sleep pressure, which builds with every hour you are awake.

Q. What is Rule 2?

A. Before I commit to a cost or a date, I write the reference-class figure beside my own estimate and explain any gap in writing.

Why this matters

Last week you learned to put the bottom line first in an email or a meeting. This week moves to the document that carries the biggest decisions: the memo you send to a partner, a lender or your own board before you commit money. A developer's decisions are usually made by people who were not in the room when the analysis was done. They decide from what you write. A long, wandering document makes them either trust you blindly or ask for a meeting to find out what you meant, and both are bad. A single page, well built, lets a busy reader make a sound decision in five minutes and leaves a record of why.

The six parts of a decision memo

In plain English: a decision memo answers six questions, in this order. What do you want me to decide? What do you recommend? Why? What else did you consider? What could go wrong? What happens next?

The professional framing is a format widely used in government briefing notes, credit papers and board papers, under various names. The headings are usually: decision required, recommendation, background, options considered, risks, and next steps, with key numbers in a small table. The order is the pyramid principle from Week 5 applied to a page: the answer first, the support beneath it, detail last.

Worked example one. A hypothetical memo to a partner, shown as its headings and first lines.

Decision required: approve an option to buy a 1-acre site for a non-refundable fee of 50,000 dollars, by 30 April.

Recommendation: approve.

Why: the option gives us 6 months to confirm zoning and soil before we commit to a purchase price of 1,500,000 dollars; the fee is about 3 percent of the price; comparable sites have sold for more.

Options considered: buy outright now, which commits 1,500,000 dollars before we know the zoning outcome; or walk away, which loses the site to another buyer.

Risks: if zoning is refused, we lose the 50,000 dollar fee; the seller may refuse to extend if studies run late.

Next steps: instruct the lawyer to draft the option agreement this week; commission the soil study on signing.

That is under 150 words. A partner can say yes or no to it in two minutes, and in a year anyone can read why you did it.

Cutting to one page

Plain English: most first drafts are three times too long because they are written in the order you did the work. Cut by moving, then by deleting.

The method is a practitioner habit with three passes. Pass one, move: put the decision and the recommendation at the top, even if you wrote them last. Pass two, delete the history: the reader needs the current state, not how you got there. Pass three, push detail out: anything a reader might want but does not need for the decision goes into an attachment, referred to by name. "Soil study attached" is a sentence. The soil study is not.

Worked example two. Suppose your first draft is 900 words. The decision appears in paragraph six. You move it to the top. You delete three paragraphs describing the site visits, which leaves 600 words. You move the zoning analysis, the comparable sales and the cash flow to attachments, leaving a three-line reference to each, and you are at about 300 words, comfortably one page. Nothing true was lost. It moved to where the reader who wants it can find it.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: decision, recommendation, why, options, risks, next steps.

"I'll confirm by Friday"

A one-page memo invites hard questions, and some of them you will not be able to answer on the spot. The most important sentence you can learn this week is the one you use then: "I don't have that figure with me. I'll confirm it in writing by Friday."

That sentence does three things. It tells the truth. It replaces a guess, which may be wrong and which the listener will remember as a fact, with a commitment. And it gives you a date by which your credibility is measured. The professional standard is that a promised confirmation arrives on time, in writing, even if the answer is "I need until Tuesday, because the engineer is still checking." A guess spoken confidently in a meeting can end up in someone's notes, in a credit paper and eventually in a dispute. A promise kept builds the reputation for reliability that every lender prices.

Consider the alternative. A partner asks what the soil study will cost, and you say, "about 20,000 dollars", from memory. The quote arrives at 32,000 dollars. You were 60 percent out on a small number, and the partner now wonders how far out you are on the big ones. Had you said, "I'll confirm by Friday", and sent the real quote on Thursday, the same partner would have learned that your figures can be relied on. The fact was identical. Only the sentence changed.

How the best do it

Some large companies have banned slide decks from their most senior meetings and require a written memo instead, read in silence at the start of the meeting so that everyone discusses the same facts. Many lenders' credit committees work from written credit papers with a fixed structure for the same reason. A small developer can copy the core of it: send the one-page memo a day ahead, ask the reader to come with questions rather than a fresh read, and keep every memo in a decision file.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a memo that omits the options you rejected and the risks you accepted. Later, when something goes wrong, the memo makes it look as though you never considered them, and you cannot show that the decision was reasoned. The control is a rule: no decision memo leaves without at least one real alternative and at least two named risks, each with what you are doing about it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes length shows effort and that a thin memo looks lazy. A reader sees the opposite: length signals that the writer has not decided what matters. The second mistake is attaching everything and summarising nothing, which makes the reader do the work you were meant to do.

Callback

In Week 2, Omar taught that a decision on the record, showing what you knew, what you weighed and why you chose, is the best evidence that you acted with care. The one-page decision memo is that record, made at the time, in a form anyone can read. Your decision journal holds your private reasoning; the memo is the version you share.

Recap

A decision memo has six parts: decision required, recommendation, why, options considered, risks and next steps. Cut a draft by moving the answer up, deleting the history and pushing detail into attachments. When you do not know a figure, say you will confirm it in writing by a date, and keep that promise.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics, on the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse and a design change that was never confirmed in writing.
checklist: Write every decision memo under the six headings: decision, recommendation, why, options, risks, next steps.
Put the decision required and the recommendation at the top, with a date.
Include at least one real alternative you rejected and why.
Name at least two risks and what you are doing about each.
Move history and supporting analysis into named attachments.
Keep the memo to one page and send it a day before the decision meeting.
When you lack a figure, promise a written confirmation by a date and deliver it on time.
head: Field checklist
speak: If I cannot put a decision on one page, I have not finished thinking about it. A decision memo answers six questions in order: what decision is required, what I recommend, why, what else I considered, what could go wrong and what happens next. That is the pyramid principle applied to a page. I cut a long draft in three passes: move the answer to the top, delete the history, and push supporting analysis into attachments referred to by name. I always include a real alternative and at least two named risks, because a memo without them makes a sound decision look careless later. I send it a day ahead so the meeting starts from the same facts. And when someone asks for a figure I do not have, I never guess. I say: I'll confirm that in writing by Friday. Then I do, on time. A guess becomes someone's fact. A kept promise becomes my reputation.
terms: Decision memo — a short document that states the decision required, a recommendation, its reasons, the options considered, the risks and the next steps.
Attachment — supporting material referred to by name in a memo but kept outside it, so the reader can find detail without wading through it.
Holding answer — a truthful statement that you will confirm a fact in writing by a stated date, used instead of a guess.

hostile.q: Your memo says comparable sites have sold for more. Which sites, and for how much?
hostile.a: I don't have the full list with me and I won't quote figures from memory. I'll send you the comparable sales schedule in writing by Friday, with addresses, dates and prices per acre. If any of them do not support the point, I will say so in that note.

title: The Hyatt Regency walkways: a change that was never confirmed
summary: In 1981 two suspended walkways at the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City collapsed during a crowded event, killing 114 people. The design change that doubled the load on a critical connection passed between firms without a calculation that anyone owned. This lesson takes the case through seven steps and ends with Rule 6.
rule: Rule 6: A change to anything that carries load or protects life is approved only in writing, by the person responsible for that design, with the check behind it; a phone call or a stamp without a check is a request, never an approval.
body:
The Hyatt Regency walkways did not fall because of an exotic force. They fell because a change to one connection travelled between two firms in conversations and drawings, and at no point did anyone write down the calculation that would have shown it could not carry the load.

Recall

Q. In Sage's worked example, what happened to profit when rent fell 10 percent?

A. It fell by more than 70 percent, because cost stayed fixed and every dollar of lost value came straight out of profit.

Q. What is Rule 4?

A. Before a critical decision I check fitness the way I check the numbers, and if the person deciding is not fit, the decision waits or changes hands.

Q. What went wrong at Berlin Brandenburg Airport, in one sentence?

A. The project skipped its gates, committing to dates and announcements before the criteria for passing each stage, above all on the fire systems, were met.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every building you develop will be changed during construction. Contractors and fabricators propose substitutions to save time or money, and most of them are fine. The danger lies in a change that alters how a structure or a life-safety system works, approved through a phone call, a hurried email or a stamp applied to a drawing nobody checked. This case is taught in engineering schools as an ethics case. For an owner it is a communication case: how a decision that should have been written, calculated and owned was instead talked about.

Step 1: Timeline

The Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, Missouri opened in 1980 with a large atrium crossed by suspended walkways. On the evening of 17 July 1981, during a crowded event in the atrium, the walkway on the fourth floor and the walkway directly beneath it on the second floor collapsed onto the people below. 114 people died and more than 200 were injured. The National Bureau of Standards investigated the structural cause. Missouri's licensing authorities later held proceedings against the structural engineers, and their licences were revoked. Read the investigation report and the licensing decision before you quote any detail; what follows is the shape of the findings.

Step 2: Key decisions

The original design hung both walkways from the ceiling on continuous steel rods. Each rod passed through the fourth-floor walkway's support beam and carried on down to the second-floor beam. Each beam was held up by a nut on the rod beneath it. The fabricator proposed a change: instead of one long rod, use two shorter ones. One set ran from the ceiling to the fourth-floor beam. A second set hung from that same fourth-floor beam down to the second-floor walkway. The change looks small on a drawing. Structurally it was not. The fourth-floor beam's connection now had to carry the fourth-floor walkway and the entire second-floor walkway hanging beneath it, roughly double its original load. The change was accepted into the shop drawings, the detailed fabrication drawings, which went back to the engineering firm and returned with its review stamp.

Step 3: Assumptions

The assumptions ran in both directions. The fabricator, by the accounts given at the hearings, understood that the engineer had accepted the change and would check it. The engineers, by their accounts, understood it differently, and testimony about a telephone conversation conflicted. Each side assumed the other had done the calculation. The investigation also found that even the original connection design fell short of the strength the building code required, which means the margin a proper check would have demanded was missing before the change made it far worse.

Step 4: Incentives

The two-rod detail was easier to fabricate and install; a continuous rod through two levels was awkward to build. The project, like most, was under schedule pressure. None of this required bad faith. A change that saves effort for the person proposing it, and costs nothing visible to the person approving it, will usually be approved unless a rule forces someone to own the check.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

There were signs during construction that the atrium structure needed attention, including an earlier partial roof failure in the atrium that prompted reviews. The opportunity to look again at every atrium connection, the walkway hangers included, was there. The deeper warning sign was procedural: a structural change was carried in drawings and conversation, without a written calculation that a named engineer had performed and signed.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: everybody thought somebody else had checked it, and nobody had written it down.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return came when the reviewed shop drawings released the fabrication. After that, the walkways were built as drawn and the defect was hidden inside a finished, painted connection. Every month of service that passed without failure made the structure feel proven, the same false comfort Ford showed you with Columbia's foam. The collapse needed only a heavy enough crowd on the walkways.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was an approval system in which responsibility for a structural change was never clearly assigned or recorded. A drawing could pass between firms, be stamped and be built without a calculation anyone owned. The technical error, a connection carrying about twice its design load on a detail that was already marginal, was the mechanism. The missing confirmation was the cause.

The prevention rule

Rule 6: A change to anything that carries load or protects life is approved only in writing, by the person responsible for that design, with the check behind it; a phone call or a stamp without a check is a request, never an approval.

Worked example one, applied. On a hypothetical project, the steel fabricator emails your project manager proposing to replace bolted connections on a transfer beam with a welded detail, to save two weeks. Your project manager replies, "Sounds good if the engineer is fine." That is not an approval; it is a hope. The Rule 6 response: "Submit the proposal as a formal substitution request. No fabrication until the engineer of record returns it approved in writing with calculations." Two weeks may still be saved, or may not. Either way, someone owns the answer.

Worked example two. Your contractor proposes substituting a cheaper fire-stopping product in service penetrations through a rated wall. It is not structural, but it protects life. Same rule: a written substitution request, the product's listing evidence and the approval of the responsible designer, recorded before installation. Professional sign-off required: the engineer of record for structural changes; the fire protection engineer or architect of record for fire-rated assemblies.

The biggest risk

On your projects the biggest risk is the verbal yes on site, given to keep the job moving. The control is a substitution and change log that every proposal must enter, with three fields that cannot be left blank: who is responsible for the design affected, the written approval and the date it was given.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats a review stamp as proof of a check. A stamp records that a document passed through someone's office. Ask what was checked, by whom, and where the calculation is.

Callback

In Week 3, Ford took you through Champlain Towers South and Rule 3: when a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, you fund and schedule the fix on the engineer's timeline. Rule 6 is its twin on the way in. Rule 3 governs what you do when an engineer warns you. Rule 6 makes sure an engineer has actually checked the change before it is built.

Recap

A fabricator's change doubled the load on a walkway connection that was already short of code strength. It passed between firms in drawings and conversation, was stamped and built, and nobody owned the calculation. Rule 6: load-bearing and life-safety changes are approved only in writing, by the responsible designer, with the check behind it.

Next: Priya, The Money, on presenting numbers aloud to a lender, and what a misstated number costs.
checklist: Require every proposed substitution or design change to arrive as a written request.
Record in a change log who is responsible for the design each change affects.
Do not release fabrication or installation until the responsible designer approves in writing.
Ask where the calculation is whenever you see a review stamp on a changed detail.
Treat life-safety items such as fire-rated assemblies under the same rule as structure.
Never give a verbal yes on site to a change that affects load or life safety.
Revisit every connection of a type that has already shown a problem on the same project.
head: Field checklist
speak: In July 1981, two suspended walkways at the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City collapsed during a crowded event, and 114 people died. The original design hung both walkways from one set of continuous rods. The fabricator proposed two shorter rods instead, which meant the fourth-floor connection carried both walkways, roughly double its load, on a detail the investigation found was already short of what the code required. The change moved between the fabricator and the engineers in drawings and conversation, the shop drawings came back stamped, and each side believed the other had done the calculation. Nobody had written it down. My rule, Rule 6: a change to anything that carries load or protects life is approved only in writing, by the person responsible for that design, with the check behind it. A phone call or a stamp without a check is a request, never an approval. On my sites, no verbal yes on those changes.
terms: Shop drawings — detailed drawings prepared by a fabricator or subcontractor showing how they will build an element, submitted for review against the design.
Engineer of record — the licensed engineer responsible for a structural or systems design on a project.
Substitution request — a formal written proposal to change a specified product, material or detail, submitted for approval before it is used.

hostile.q: Your contractor says the engineer agreed the welded detail on a site visit. Why are you holding up fabrication?
hostile.a: Because a site conversation is not an approval for a structural change. I have asked for a formal substitution request, and the engineer of record will return it approved in writing with calculations. If that takes three days, we lose three days. We are not building a transfer connection that nobody has checked on paper.

title: Numbers aloud: what a lender hears, and what a misstated number costs
summary: Lenders size loans and set terms from the numbers you give them, and a number said carelessly is remembered as a fact. This lesson sets five rules for presenting numbers aloud, works through a monthly-versus-annual mistake and a percent-versus-percentage-point mistake, and prices what lost credibility costs at the credit committee.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a lender writes down the number you say, not the number you meant. Say every figure with its unit, its period and a comparison, and round it to what a listener can hold.

Recall

Q. In a first land meeting, what do you do after the owner names a figure?

A. Pause before responding, so your reply is chosen rather than reflexive, and ask about it before you react to it.

Q. How did Roman price a tired mistake?

A. As expected cost, the chance of an error times what it costs, plus the carrying cost of the delay it causes.

Q. What does optimism cost a project, in Priya's Week 2 lesson?

A. Delay and carry: an optimistic schedule that slips adds interest and overhead every week, and slow decisions add more.

Why this matters

A lender's first view of your project often comes from a conversation, not a document: a call with a relationship manager, a meeting at a site, a short presentation to a credit team. The numbers you say in those conversations become the lender's working assumptions. If one of them is wrong, two things happen. The analysis is built on a bad figure, and when the error surfaces, as it will when your written package arrives, the lender's trust in every other number you gave falls with it. Trust is not free. It shows up in loan terms.

Five rules for numbers aloud

Plain English, the rules. One: always say the unit. Not "nine point nine", but "nine point nine million dollars". Two: always say the period. Rent per month or per year, interest per year, cost per square foot or per square metre. Three: round to about two significant figures, the first two digits that carry meaning, and keep exact figures on paper. Four: one number per sentence, so the listener can write it down. Five: give a comparison, because a number alone has no meaning to someone who has not seen your model: "Operating expenses are about 35 percent of income, in line with similar buildings nearby."

The professional framing is that spoken numbers are processed far less reliably than written ones. The listener cannot reread. This is why credit teams and good analysts say a figure, pause, and repeat it in a different form: "About 593,000 dollars a year, so roughly 49,000 dollars a month."

One more habit belongs here. When a figure is genuinely uncertain, say a range and say what drives it: "Construction cost is between 8.2 and 8.8 million dollars, depending on the foundation design, which we will know in two weeks." A single confident figure for an uncertain quantity is a promise you cannot keep. A range with its driver tells the lender exactly where the risk sits, and it is the spoken form of Rule 5.

The monthly-versus-annual trap

Worked example one. A hypothetical building produces net operating income, or NOI, the income after operating expenses and before loan payments, of 592,800 dollars a year. That is 49,400 dollars a month. On a call you say, "NOI is about 49 thousand", meaning per month. The relationship manager writes "NOI 49,000", and in her files every income figure is annual.

Here is why that matters. As a matter of commercial practice, not a standard, many lenders size a loan so that the property's yearly NOI covers the yearly loan payments by a cushion, for example 1.25 times. Week 36 teaches this properly as the debt service coverage ratio. Run the hypothetical. With the correct annual NOI of 592,800 dollars, the maximum yearly payment is 592,800 divided by 1.25, which equals 474,240 dollars. With the misheard 49,000 dollars as annual NOI, the maximum yearly payment is 49,000 divided by 1.25, which equals 39,200 dollars, about one twelfth as much. The lender's first rough sizing of your loan is a fraction of what the building can support. You will correct it, but you have started the relationship with a figure off by a factor of twelve, and the lender now checks everything twice.

The fix costs four words: "about 49 thousand a month, so about 593 thousand a year."

The percent-versus-percentage-point trap

Plain English: when a rate moves from 6 percent to 6.5 percent, it has risen by half a percentage point. It has also risen by about 8 percent of itself, because 0.5 divided by 6 is about 0.083. Both statements are true. Saying "it went up half a percent" is ambiguous, and in finance ambiguity about rates costs money.

Worked example two. You tell a lender, "If cap rates rise half a percent, value drops about 7 or 8 percent." The lender hears "half a percent" as 6 percent times 1.005, which is 6.03 percent, a trivial move, and concludes your project is insensitive to cap rates. It is not. Using last week's hypothetical, NOI of 592,800 dollars at a 6 percent cap rate is worth 9,880,000 dollars, and at 6.5 percent it is worth 9,120,000 dollars, a fall of 760,000 dollars, about 7.7 percent. The correct sentence: "If cap rates rise half a percentage point, from 6 to 6.5, value falls about 760,000 dollars, nearly 8 percent." Now the lender has the size of the risk, not a misleading impression of it.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: unit, period, round, one number per sentence, compare.

What lost credibility costs

Credibility is not on any pro forma, but you can estimate its price. When a credit committee is uneasy about a sponsor's numbers, it does not usually refuse outright. It tightens terms. It may ask for a larger equity contribution, a larger reserve, more frequent reporting or a higher margin, the lender's spread over its base rate. These are commercial outcomes that vary by lender and market, not standards.

A hypothetical illustration. On a 6,000,000 dollar loan, an extra quarter of a percentage point of margin costs 6,000,000 times 0.0025, which equals 15,000 dollars a year. Over a three-year loan that is about 45,000 dollars, before any extra reserve or reporting cost. A careless number in a first meeting that leads to one notch of tighter terms can cost more than a year of a junior analyst's time spent checking every figure before it is said. That is the business case for preparing your numbers before the call.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is saying a number you have not checked because the moment seems to want one. The control is a one-page number sheet, prepared before any lender or investor conversation, with each key figure stated with its unit, its period and its source. If a figure is not on the sheet, it is a "confirm by Friday" figure, and you say so.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks reciting exact figures shows command of the deal. A string of seven-digit numbers said aloud shows only that the speaker has not decided which ones matter. Command is the rounded figure, its comparison, and the exact figure available on paper the moment someone asks.

Callback

In Week 3 you learned anchoring: the first number on the table pulls every estimate after it. The numbers you say in a first lender conversation are anchors too, and a wrong anchor drags the lender's whole view of your deal. Rule 5 from last week applies here as well: if a number carries a risk, such as the sensitivity of value to the cap rate, say the risk in the same breath as the number.

Recap

Say every number with its unit and its period, round it, say one per sentence and compare it with something. Confirm monthly versus annual out loud. Distinguish percent from percentage points. A misstated number damages trust, and trust is priced in equity, reserves, reporting and margin. Prepare a number sheet before every lender conversation. All figures here are hypothetical.

Next: Vera, The Rules, on the written record: confirming emails, notes made at the time and why "I'll confirm by Friday" belongs in writing.
checklist: Prepare a one-page number sheet with unit, period and source before every lender call.
Say every number with its unit and its period.
Round spoken figures to about two significant figures.
State monthly and annual versions of income figures together.
Use percentage points for changes in rates, and give the effect in dollars.
Pair each key number with a comparison to a benchmark.
Treat any figure not on your sheet as a confirm-by-Friday item.
head: Field checklist
speak: A lender writes down the number I say, not the number I meant. So I follow five rules. I always say the unit. I always say the period, per month or per year. I round to about two significant figures and keep the exact figures on paper. I say one number per sentence. And I compare each number with something, so it means something. Two traps matter most. Monthly versus annual: if I say NOI is about 49 thousand, meaning a month, and the lender files it as a year, her first rough sizing of my loan is off by a factor of twelve. And percent versus percentage points: a cap rate going from 6 to 6.5 is half a percentage point, and on my hypothetical building it takes about 760,000 dollars off value. A misstated number costs trust, and lenders price lost trust as tighter terms, which on a 6 million dollar loan can mean 15,000 dollars a year for a quarter point.
terms: Significant figures — the digits in a number that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit; two is usually enough when speaking.
Percentage point — the unit for the arithmetic difference between two percentages, such as 6 percent to 6.5 percent being half a percentage point.
Margin (lending) — the spread a lender charges above its base rate, set by commercial terms rather than any standard.

hostile.q: On the phone you told us NOI was 49,000. Your package says 593,000. Which is it?
hostile.a: Both describe the same building: 49,400 dollars a month, which is 592,800 dollars a year. I should have said the period on the call, and that is my error. Every income figure in the package is annual, and each one is sourced on the attached number sheet so your team can check it.

title: The written record: confirming emails, notes made at the time, and version control
summary: When a project ends in dispute, what was said matters less than what can be shown. This lesson explains why records made at the time carry weight, how to write a confirming email after a call, how to keep minutes and an action log that survive scrutiny, and why the version of a document matters as much as its content.
body:
Mr Shabazz, memory fades and disagrees; a record made at the time does not. Every important conversation on your project should end in writing within a day, in words the other side had the chance to correct.

Recall

Q. What does the Red Pen drill train you to catch?

A. Planted defects in a short document, such as a buried request, a hedged ask, a risk below a reassurance and a casual yes, so you catch them in real work.

Q. Does tiredness excuse a commitment you made by email?

A. Generally no. A commitment usually binds however tired you were, which is why the red window keeps signatures and approvals out of your worst hours.

Q. What does a pre-mortem ask?

A. It asks the team to imagine the project has already failed and write down why, before the decision, so hidden risks surface in time to act.

Why this matters

Construction disputes, insurance claims and lender defaults are decided long after the events, by people who were not there: an adjudicator, an arbitrator, a judge, an insurer's adjuster or a lender's workout team. They reconstruct what happened from documents. A developer with a clear, consistent record made at the time is in a far stronger position than one relying on recollection, however honest. This is not about building a case against your partners. It is about running a project where everyone can see what was agreed. How records are treated as evidence depends on the forum and the jurisdiction, so this lesson teaches habits and concepts, not legal rules. Verify specific requirements with a lawyer.

Why records made at the time carry weight

Plain English: a note written straight after a meeting is usually more believable than an account written months later, because it was made before anyone knew there would be a dispute and before memory shifted to fit an interest.

The professional framing is the contemporaneous record: a document created at or close to the time of the event it describes, in the ordinary course of business. In many systems, decision makers give such records significant weight, especially when they were shared with the other party at the time and not challenged. A record that was sent and not disputed tells a later reader that the other side, at the time, accepted it. Verify how that works in the forum that applies before you rely on it.

The confirming email

The single most useful habit on a project is the confirming email: after any call or meeting where something is decided, you send a short written note of what was agreed, asking the other side to correct anything wrong.

Worked example one. A hypothetical call with your contractor about a delayed concrete pour. Without a record, you each remember it your own way. With one, you send this the same afternoon:

Further to our call at 14:00 today, my understanding is: 1. The level 3 slab pour moves from 10 to 14 June because of the late rebar delivery. 2. You are not claiming extra time or cost for this change; you will recover it within the existing programme. 3. You will send a revised three-week look-ahead by Friday. If any of this is not your understanding, please tell me by Wednesday.

Look at what it does. It is numbered, so each point can be agreed or disputed separately. It states dates, not "next week". It records the point that matters most later, whether a claim is being made. It sets a deadline for correction. If the contractor says nothing, you have a contemporaneous record he received and did not challenge. If he replies that he is claiming time, you have learned that today, while the facts are fresh and you can still act.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: further to our call, my understanding is, please correct me by Wednesday.

Minutes, action logs and the decision log

Plain English: minutes record what a meeting decided, not everything said in it. An action log tracks each task agreed: what, who and by when, and whether it is done.

Worked example two. Suppose, as a hypothetical, six months into construction the contractor claims that you instructed acceleration at a site meeting in March and owes the cost of extra crews. You say you asked only whether acceleration was possible. If your March minutes read, "Owner asked contractor to price acceleration options for decision at April meeting. Action: contractor, price by 2 April," and those minutes were circulated and not corrected, you have strong evidence of what happened. If there are no minutes, it is your word against the contractor's, and his crews' timesheets show they were on site.

Three rules make minutes worth having. Circulate them within two working days. Record decisions and actions, with owners and dates, not a transcript. And open every meeting by confirming the previous minutes, or noting the corrections, so that the record is accepted as it goes. Your owner decision log, which you will meet properly in Week 48, works the same way: each decision, the date, who decided, the reason and the memo it rests on.

Version control and "I'll confirm by Friday"

A record is only useful if you can tell which version was the live one. Version control means every important document carries a version number and date, superseded versions are marked as superseded, and only one current version is circulated. Disputes are often about which drawing revision the contractor priced, or which version of a term sheet the lender approved. A file named "final", "final 2" and "final revised" invites exactly that argument. Keep it findable as well: one project folder, a consistent naming pattern such as date, document, version, and correspondence filed by subject. A record you cannot find in an hour, when the lender or an adjudicator asks for it, is worth little more than no record at all.

The holding answer from Day 1, "I'll confirm by Friday", belongs in this system too. Put it in the action log as an action on you, with the date. When you send the confirmation, refer to the question and the meeting it came from. A promise to confirm that is recorded and kept becomes evidence of a reliable process. One that is forgotten becomes evidence of the opposite.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the decision made in conversation and never written: a price, a scope change or an extension agreed on the phone. The control is a twenty-four-hour rule: any decision made orally is confirmed in writing within one working day, numbered and dated, with a deadline for correction. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer, before any record is created or altered once a dispute is expected, because rules about preserving documents may then apply.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks writing things down signals distrust. Experienced contractors and lenders read it as professionalism, and most prefer it, because the record protects them too. The second mistake is the opposite: writing emotional, speculative or accusatory notes in project correspondence. Anything you write may be read later by the other side. Write facts, decisions and actions.

Callback

In Week 5, LEX showed that a short reply can bind you and that notices must follow the contract's clause. Records are the other half of that lesson. LEX taught you to choose your words because they may be treated as a commitment. Vera adds: make sure the commitments you intend are written down, confirmed and findable, because what you cannot show, you may not be able to rely on.

Recap

Records made at the time, shared and not challenged, usually carry weight. Confirm every oral decision in writing within a day, numbered, dated and with a correction deadline. Keep minutes of decisions and actions, circulated quickly and confirmed at the next meeting. Control versions. Put every "I'll confirm by Friday" in the action log and keep it.

Next: Nadia, The Numbers, working backward from the equity a memo asks for to the assumption hidden inside it.
checklist: Send a numbered confirming email within one working day of any oral decision.
Include a date by which the other side should correct anything wrong.
Record whether any claim for time or money is being made in every confirming note.
Circulate minutes of decisions and actions within two working days.
Confirm or correct the previous minutes at the start of every meeting.
Give every important document a version number and date, and mark superseded versions.
Log every confirm-by-Friday promise as an action on yourself and close it on time.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a project ends in dispute, what was said matters less than what can be shown. A record made at the time, shared with the other side and not challenged, usually carries weight, because it was written before anyone had a reason to bend it. So after any call where something is decided, I send a confirming email the same day: further to our call, my understanding is, then numbered points with dates, including whether any claim for time or money is being made, and a deadline for corrections. I keep minutes of decisions and actions, not transcripts, circulate them within two working days and confirm them at the next meeting. I control versions so everyone knows which drawing or term sheet is live. And every time I say I'll confirm by Friday, it goes in the action log as my action. How records are treated as evidence depends on the forum, so I check specifics with a lawyer.
terms: Contemporaneous record — a document made at or near the time of the event it describes, in the ordinary course of business.
Confirming email — a short written note sent after a conversation, setting out what was agreed and inviting correction by a date.
Version control — the practice of numbering and dating documents and marking superseded versions so only one current version is in use.

hostile.q: You say you never instructed acceleration. Can you prove it?
hostile.a: Yes. The minutes of the March meeting record that I asked you to price acceleration options for decision in April, with an action on you to price them by 2 April. Those minutes were circulated two days later and confirmed without correction at the April meeting. I have no record of any instruction to accelerate, and nor, I think, do you.

title: Reverse engineering the ask: from the equity a memo requests to the assumption hidden inside it
summary: A single number at the top of a memo usually rests on an assumption nobody stated. This lesson starts from a hypothetical request for 1,500,000 dollars of new equity and works backward, step by step, to the loan assumption it implies, then works back again to what the cost increase does to profit and to the return on the partners' money.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when a memo hands you a number, work backward from it until you find the assumption that produced it. Most bad decisions are made on a correct calculation from an assumption nobody said out loud.

Recall

Q. What are the six parts of a decision memo?

A. Decision required, recommendation, why, options considered, risks and next steps.

Q. How did Petra plan a sharp two o'clock after night shifts?

A. She started from the meeting time and worked backward to set sleep, light exposure and the last caffeine, so the decision landed in a good hour.

Q. What does working backward from the margin tell you?

A. Starting from the profit you need, it tells you the most the project can cost, which is the estimate you can afford, before you see the contractor's number.

Why this matters

This week is about memos and presenting numbers. The other side of writing a good memo is reading one well, including your own team's. A memo's headline number is the thing the reader is asked to approve. If that number quietly assumes something, such as that the lender will not increase the loan, that the sale price holds or that interest costs do not change, approving the number approves the assumption. Reverse engineering is how you make the assumption visible before you sign.

All figures in this lesson are hypothetical and round, and interest and fees are simplified so the logic shows. Loan-to-cost limits and profit targets are commercial practice that varies by lender and market, not standards.

The memo

Your project manager sends a one-page memo. Decision required: "Approve an additional 1,500,000 dollars of partner equity by 30 June." Why: "The contractor's revised price takes total development cost from 10,000,000 to 11,500,000 dollars." You know the original financing: a loan of 6,500,000 dollars and partner equity of 3,500,000 dollars. The memo is well structured. Now test the number.

Worked example one: the hidden loan assumption

Step 1. Start from the finished outcome: new equity of 1,500,000 dollars.

Step 2. Total cost is always funded by debt plus equity. So new total equity would be 3,500,000 plus 1,500,000, which equals 5,000,000 dollars.

Step 3. Work back to the implied loan. Total cost of 11,500,000 minus equity of 5,000,000 equals 6,500,000 dollars. The memo assumes the loan does not move at all.

Step 4. Ask whether that is true. The original loan was 6,500,000 on a cost of 10,000,000, so loan-to-cost, meaning the loan as a share of total cost, was 65 percent. If the lender's commitment allows lending up to 65 percent of cost, and the lender will accept the higher cost, the loan could rise to 11,500,000 times 0.65, which equals 7,475,000 dollars.

Step 5. Rework the equity under that alternative. Equity needed: 11,500,000 minus 7,475,000 equals 4,025,000 dollars. New equity required: 4,025,000 minus 3,500,000 equals 525,000 dollars.

So the same cost increase needs either 1,500,000 or 525,000 dollars of new equity, depending entirely on a lender assumption the memo never stated. The difference, 975,000 dollars, is larger than the smaller request. Neither answer is automatically right. A lender may refuse to increase the loan, may require new appraisal support, or may impose conditions. But the decision you are asked to make is really about the loan, and the memo did not say so.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: the equity number is the cost increase minus whatever the lender will add.

Worked example two: back from the cost increase to profit and return

The memo also omits what the increase does to returns, which the six-part structure would have caught under Risks. Work it backward from the value.

Step 1. Assume a hypothetical completed value of 13,000,000 dollars, which does not change with cost.

Step 2. Original profit: 13,000,000 minus 10,000,000 equals 3,000,000 dollars. Original profit on cost: 3,000,000 divided by 10,000,000, which is 30 percent.

Step 3. Revised profit: 13,000,000 minus 11,500,000 equals 1,500,000 dollars. Revised profit on cost: 1,500,000 divided by 11,500,000, which is about 13 percent. The cost rose 15 percent; profit halved.

Step 4. Now look at it from the partners' side. Under the memo's assumption, partners put in 5,000,000 dollars of equity and the project makes 1,500,000 dollars of profit: 1,500,000 divided by 5,000,000 is 30 percent profit on equity, against 3,000,000 divided by 3,500,000, about 86 percent, originally. Under the alternative, with the larger loan, partners put in 4,025,000 dollars for the same 1,500,000 dollars of profit, about 37 percent. A larger loan would also carry more interest, which this simplified example leaves out; in a real model that would reduce the profit. The point stands: the financing assumption changes the partners' return materially.

Step 5. Work back one more step to a decision rule. Suppose the partners require at least 15 percent profit on cost before committing more money. That is a commercial threshold, not a standard. Then the maximum cost the project can bear is value divided by 1.15: 13,000,000 divided by 1.15 equals about 11,300,000 dollars. The revised cost of 11,500,000 is about 200,000 dollars over that limit. Before anyone approves new equity, the project needs about 200,000 dollars of savings, a higher value supported by evidence, or a decision to accept a lower threshold.

The five-minute reverse check

You will not always have time to rebuild a model. Here is a practitioner routine you can run in five minutes with a phone calculator, before any meeting where you are asked to approve money.

  1. Write the requested number and its unit at the top of a blank page.
  2. Write the identity it must obey. For funding, cost equals debt plus equity. For value, value equals NOI divided by the cap rate. For profit, profit equals value minus cost.
  3. Fill in every other term from the memo or from what you already know. The one left over is the assumption.
  4. Change that assumption to the most plausible alternative and recompute.
  5. Write one sentence: "This request assumes X; if instead Y, the number is Z."

That sentence becomes your first question in the meeting, and it is a better question than any about the arithmetic. It moves the discussion from whether the number is right to whether the assumption is right, which is where the money is decided. If the memo's author already considered the alternative, you have lost nothing and gained confidence. If not, you have found the real decision before you made it by accident.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is approving a well-formatted number without rebuilding it. Good structure can make an incomplete analysis look complete. The control is a two-line reverse check on every money request: what does this number imply about each funding source, and what does it do to profit on cost and to the return on equity? If the memo does not answer both, send it back with those two questions, or answer them yourself before the meeting.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner checks the arithmetic and stops. The arithmetic in this memo was correct: 11,500,000 minus 10,000,000 really is 1,500,000. The beginner's mistake is assuming that correct arithmetic means a correct number. The number was only as good as the assumption that the loan stayed fixed, and that assumption was the real decision.

Callback

In Week 5, Sage built a bottom line forward, from rent to income to value to profit, and found the three inputs it depended on. This lesson ran the same chain the other way, from a requested number back to its inputs. Forward tells you what a project produces. Backward tells you what a number is quietly assuming. On every memo that asks for money, run both.

Recap

Start from the number you are asked to approve. Split it into its sources, debt and equity, and see what it implies about each. Rework it under the alternative assumption. Then work back from value to profit on cost and to return on equity, and from your required threshold to the maximum cost the project can bear. Approve assumptions, not only numbers.

Next: Kema, The Room, on hostile questions from an investor: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and never guess.
checklist: For every money request, split the number into its debt and equity sources.
Write down the funding assumption the number implies, and test the alternative.
Rework the request under the alternative and record the difference.
Calculate the effect on profit on cost and on return on equity.
Work back from your required threshold to the maximum cost the project can bear.
Send back any memo that omits the effect on returns, with that question attached.
Confirm with the lender, in writing, any loan assumption a decision depends on.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a memo hands me a number, I work backward until I find the assumption behind it. A hypothetical memo asks for 1,500,000 dollars of new equity because cost has gone from 10 million to 11.5 million. Cost is funded by debt plus equity, so that number only works if the loan stays at 6.5 million. If the lender would keep lending 65 percent of cost, the loan could rise to about 7.5 million and new equity would be about 525,000 dollars. The real decision is about the loan, and the memo never said so. Then I work back from value. On a 13 million dollar completed value, profit falls from 3 million to 1.5 million, from 30 percent on cost to about 13 percent. If the partners need 15 percent, the most the project can cost is about 11.3 million, so we need about 200,000 dollars of savings first. I approve assumptions, not just numbers.
terms: Loan-to-cost (LTC) — the loan as a percentage of total development cost; limits are set by commercial lending terms, not standards.
Return on equity — profit divided by the equity invested, here measured simply over the life of the project.
Reverse check — working backward from a stated number to the assumptions that must be true for it to hold.

hostile.q: Your memo asks us for 1.5 million more. Why should the partners carry all of the overrun?
hostile.a: You should not take that as given. The 1.5 million assumes the lender adds nothing. If the lender will fund 65 percent of the higher cost, new equity falls to about 525,000. I am asking the lender in writing this week, and I will bring both cases to the decision. Separately, we are about 200,000 dollars over the cost at which we still clear 15 percent on cost, so I am also bringing savings options.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: The hostile question: acknowledge, bridge, answer
summary: Sooner or later an investor or lender will ask a question designed to rattle you. This lesson sets a realistic partner meeting about a cost overrun and teaches the acknowledge, bridge, answer method, the lines to say and never to say, the question behind the hostile question, when to stay silent and how to keep your state when the room turns cold.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a hostile question is rarely about the words in it. It is a test of whether you will defend yourself or deal with the problem. Acknowledge what is true, bridge to what matters, answer with a fact or a dated promise, and stop talking.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 6?

A. A change to anything that carries load or protects life is approved only in writing, by the person responsible for that design, with the check behind it; a phone call or a stamp without a check is a request, never an approval.

Q. What two tools from Week 4 steady you before a hard answer?

A. Slow breathing, done only when seated or parked, and reappraisal, relabelling a racing heart as energy for the task rather than as a warning.

Q. What are the four questions of an after-action review?

A. What was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why there was a difference, and what we will do next time.

Why this matters

A developer's credibility is set less by how he presents good news than by how he handles bad news under pressure. Partners and lenders know projects go wrong. What they are measuring in a hard meeting is whether you see the problem clearly, take responsibility for your part, and have a plan. A defensive answer, a guess or a long justification tells them the opposite, and they will price it into the next deal or quietly decide there will not be one.

The scene

A hypothetical. You are presenting the cost-overrun memo from yesterday's lesson to three equity partners. Revised cost has risen from 10,000,000 to 11,500,000 dollars. The most experienced partner, who has been quiet, leans forward: "This is the second budget increase this year. Why should we believe your numbers this time?"

The room goes still. Every instinct says explain, defend, list the reasons the contractor's price moved. Resist that. Count one slow breath, and use the method.

Acknowledge, bridge, answer

Plain English: first say what is true in the question. Then connect it to the point that actually matters. Then give a direct answer: a fact, a number or a dated commitment.

The professional framing is a widely taught media and negotiation technique, often called acknowledge, bridge, answer, or a close variant. The acknowledgement lowers the temperature because you have agreed with something rather than resisted. The bridge stops you being trapped inside the questioner's framing. The answer proves you are not using the bridge to dodge. Without the answer, the technique becomes the politician's evasion, and experienced investors recognise it instantly.

Worked example one. Applied to the partner's question.

Acknowledge: "That's a fair challenge. It is the second increase, and the first one was my estimate being wrong on site works."

Bridge: "The question that matters is whether this number is more reliable than the last, and why."

Answer: "This one is a contractor's fixed price for the structure, not an estimate, and it holds until 20 March. The remaining open items are listed in the memo with ranges. The biggest is foundations, between zero and 200,000 dollars, which we will know when the boreholes report in two weeks."

Then stop. Do not add a fourth or fifth sentence of justification. Silence after a good answer tells the room you have finished, and invites the next real question.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: that's fair; the question that matters is; here is the answer.

Lines to say, lines never to say

Say: "You're right that..." when they are. Say: "I don't know that figure. I'll confirm it in writing by Friday." Say: "Here is what I would do differently." Say: "Let me answer the first part, then come back to the second."

Never say: "With respect..." which signals the opposite. Never say "As I already said", which tells the listener they were not paying attention. Never blame a named person in the room or a party who is absent; the partners will wonder what you say about them elsewhere. Never guess a number to fill a silence, because a guess said with confidence becomes the figure in their notes. And never promise an outcome you do not control, such as "the lender will definitely agree".

The question behind the hostile question

Worked example two. A second partner says, sharply, "Are you even watching the contractor, or just paying invoices?" The literal question is about supervision. The question behind it is usually fear: "Am I going to lose my money, and would I find out in time?" Answering only the literal question, with a description of your site visits, misses the fear. Answer both: "Fair question. I'm on site twice a week and an independent cost consultant reviews every payment application before I approve it. More to the point, from this month you will get a one-page cost report on the first of every month, showing budget, committed cost and forecast, so you see any movement as soon as I do." The second half answers the fear with a control the partner can verify.

When you cannot tell what lies behind a question, ask. "Before I answer, is your concern the size of this increase or whether there will be more?" A clarifying question is not an evasion if you then answer.

Holding your state

A cold room raises your heart rate and speeds your speech. Keep both feet on the floor, take one slow breath before you answer, and lower your pace by a notch. Reappraise the jolt as readiness rather than threat. If you feel anger, notice it and do not let it into your voice; the person who stays calm usually ends up running the meeting. These are practitioner habits drawn from research on stress and performance; check any persistent physical symptoms with your doctor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is answering the emotion with emotion: defending, over-explaining or counter-attacking. The control is rehearsal. Before any hard meeting, write the three most hostile questions you could be asked, draft the acknowledge, bridge and answer for each, and say them aloud twice. The questions are rarely a surprise; only your composure is.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner uses the bridge and skips the answer. "That's a great question, and what really matters is our strong pipeline" is evasion, and it costs more credibility than the original bad news. The second mistake is apologising at length. One clear sentence of ownership is enough; more sounds like you are asking for comfort.

Personal brand

Your personal brand as a developer is not a logo or a feed. It is what lenders, partners, contractors and officials say about you when you are not in the room, and it is built almost entirely in moments like this one: how you deliver bad news, whether your confirmations arrive when you said, whether your numbers survive checking.

So decide on purpose what you want those people to say, in one sentence, and test your behaviour against it. A useful candidate: "His numbers hold up, and when they move, he tells you first." Every kept Friday promise adds to it. Every guess that turns out wrong subtracts more than a kept promise adds.

Callback

In Week 3 you learned that loss aversion makes people feel a loss more sharply than an equal gain. A partner hearing about an overrun is feeling a loss, and that is why the question arrives with an edge. Acknowledging it is not weakness. It is meeting the feeling with the fact, which is the only thing that settles it.

Recap

Breathe, acknowledge what is true, bridge to what matters, answer with a fact or a dated promise, and stop. Look for the fear behind the question and answer it with a control the other side can check. Never guess, blame or promise what you do not control. Rehearse your three worst questions.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap, with six questions, a Red Pen drill on a one-page memo and the two-minute boardroom drill.
checklist: Write the three most hostile questions you could face before any hard meeting.
Draft an acknowledge, bridge and answer reply to each and say them aloud twice.
Take one slow breath before answering a hostile question.
Always finish with a fact, a number or a dated commitment, then stop talking.
Replace any guess with: I'll confirm it in writing by Friday.
Answer the fear behind the question with a control the other side can verify.
Write one sentence describing what you want lenders and partners to say about you.
head: Field checklist
speak: A hostile question is usually a test of whether I will defend myself or deal with the problem. So I take one slow breath and use acknowledge, bridge, answer. I acknowledge what is true: that's fair, it is the second increase. I bridge to what matters: the real question is whether this number is more reliable. Then I answer with a fact or a dated promise: this is a fixed price that holds until a set date, and the one open item is foundations, which we will know in two weeks. Then I stop. Without the answer, the technique is just evasion. I look for the fear behind the question, usually will I lose my money and will I find out in time, and I answer it with a control the partner can check, like a monthly one-page cost report. I never guess, never blame and never promise what I do not control. I rehearse my three worst questions before the meeting.
terms: Acknowledge, bridge, answer — a technique for hard questions: state what is true in the question, connect it to what matters, then give a direct answer.
Hostile question — a question asked with an edge, often to test composure or to express a fear, rather than only to obtain information.
Personal brand — what lenders, partners, contractors and officials say about you when you are not in the room.

hostile.q: This is your second budget increase this year. Why should we believe your numbers this time?
hostile.a: That's a fair challenge; the first increase was my estimate being wrong on site works. What matters is whether this number is more reliable. It is a contractor's fixed price for the structure, holding until 20 March. The one material open item is foundations, between zero and 200,000 dollars, and we will know in two weeks. From this month you will get a one-page cost report on the first of every month.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 6 review: memos, numbers aloud, hostile questions and the Red Pen
summary: Six questions on the week, a one-page recap, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical decision memo with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom explanation of how written memos, careful numbers and honest answers protect a developer's money and reputation.
body:
This week's single idea: put decisions on one page, say numbers so they cannot be misheard, confirm in writing what was agreed, and meet hard questions with a fact or a dated promise rather than a guess. Today you test it, mark up a memo and say the week aloud in two minutes.

Recall

Q. What is the question behind a hostile question about supervision?

A. Usually fear: will I lose my money, and would I find out in time? Answer it with a control the other side can verify.

Q. What is a red window?

A. A written rule naming the hours, such as overnight and straight after a night shift, when you will not sign, pay or make new commitments.

Q. What does a gate meeting decide?

A. Whether the next block of money and time is committed, against written criteria agreed before the gate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Week 5 taught you to speak with the answer first. Week 6 put that discipline into the documents and moments that carry the most money: the memo, the spoken number, the confirming email and the hard question. Answer each question below aloud before reading the answer. Mark any you hesitated on, reread that day's lesson only, and come back to all six in a week without looking.

The six questions

Question 1: What are the six parts of a decision memo?

Answer: Decision required, recommendation, why, options considered, risks and next steps.

Question 2: What is Rule 6?

Answer: A change to anything that carries load or protects life is approved only in writing, by the person responsible for that design, with the check behind it; a phone call or a stamp without a check is a request, never an approval.

Question 3: You say NOI is about 49 thousand on a call. What is missing, and why does it matter?

Answer: The period. If you meant per month and the lender files it as per year, her rough loan sizing is off by a factor of twelve; say both: about 49 thousand a month, about 593 thousand a year.

Question 4: What makes a confirming email useful as a record?

Answer: It is sent within a day, numbers each point, states dates, records whether any claim is being made, and sets a deadline for the other side to correct it.

Question 5: A memo asks for 1,500,000 dollars of new equity after cost rises from 10,000,000 to 11,500,000 on a 6,500,000 dollar loan. What does it assume?

Answer: That the loan does not increase. If the lender keeps lending 65 percent of cost, the loan rises to 7,475,000 dollars and new equity falls to 525,000 dollars.

Question 6: What are the three steps for a hostile question, and what makes the method honest?

Answer: Acknowledge what is true, bridge to what matters, then answer with a fact or a dated commitment. The answer is what makes it honest; without it the method is evasion.

The week in one page

Day 1 gave the six-part decision memo, the three-pass cut to one page, and the holding answer: I'll confirm it in writing by Friday. Day 2, Ford took the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse through seven steps: a fabricator's change doubled the load on a connection already short of code strength, passed between firms in drawings and conversation, was stamped and built, and nobody owned the calculation. Day 3, Priya set five rules for numbers aloud and showed how monthly versus annual and percent versus percentage points mislead a lender, and how lost credibility is priced in terms. Day 4, Vera explained why records made at the time carry weight and built the confirming email, minutes, action log and version control. Day 5, Nadia reverse engineered an equity request to the loan assumption hidden inside it. Day 6 put you in front of a hostile partner with acknowledge, bridge, answer, and added the thread on personal brand.

The Red Pen

Here is a hypothetical decision memo. Read it twice and mark every defect before reading on.

Project update and request. Background: since the project began in January we have worked closely with the contractor, the engineer and the lender, and there have been a number of developments. The steel fabricator suggested a different connection on the transfer beam, which the engineer said sounded fine on site, so we have gone ahead to save time. The contractor's price has moved and total cost is now around 11 and a half. We therefore need 1.5 million from the partners. Returns remain attractive. Please approve.

Say that out loud now.

Say each defect aloud as you find it, then compare.

The defects. First, there is no decision required at the top and no date: the request appears in the fifth sentence and the approval has no deadline. Second, it opens with history, which the reader does not need. Third, and most serious, "the engineer said sounded fine on site, so we have gone ahead" breaks Rule 6: a structural change has been released for fabrication on a verbal remark, with no written approval and no calculation. That is a stop-work item, not a line in an update. Fourth, "around 11 and a half" has no unit and no exact figure, the kind of spoken number Priya warned about, in writing. Fifth, the 1.5 million request hides the assumption that the loan does not increase, and gives no alternative. Sixth, "returns remain attractive" is a reassurance with no number: the effect on profit on cost and on return on equity is missing. Seventh, there are no risks and no next steps.

The rewrite begins: "Decision required: none today on equity. Action taken: I have stopped fabrication of the transfer-beam connection until the engineer of record approves the change in writing with calculations. Separately, cost has risen from 10,000,000 to 11,500,000 dollars; I will bring a decision memo by 30 June with two funding cases, with and without a larger loan, and the effect on returns."

The boardroom drill

Set a timer for two minutes and explain this week to an imagined board. Then compare with the model.

Model answer: "Our decisions are made from paper, so the paper has to carry them. Every decision comes to you as a one-page memo: the decision required with a date, the recommendation, the reasons, the options we rejected, the risks and the next steps. Every number we give a lender is said with its unit and its period and backed by a number sheet, because one misheard figure costs trust, and trust is priced into loan terms. Every decision made in conversation is confirmed in writing within a day. Any change to structure or fire protection is approved only in writing by the responsible designer, with calculations; the Hyatt Regency collapse is why. And when we are asked something we do not know, we do not guess. We confirm it in writing by a date, and we keep that promise."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after this week is keeping the habits for formal documents and dropping them on the phone and on site, where most decisions are actually made. The control is the twenty-four-hour confirming email, applied to every call that decides anything.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats memos, minutes and confirmations as paperwork that slows the work. They are the work. They are how a project that runs for years keeps one version of the truth.

Callback

In Week 2, Omar taught that a decision on the record, showing what you knew and why you chose, is the best evidence that you acted with care. This week built that record piece by piece: the memo before the decision, the confirming email after the call, the minutes after the meeting and the kept Friday promise.

Recap

One page for every decision. Numbers with units, periods and comparisons. Confirm in writing within a day. Rule 6 for any change to structure or life safety. Reverse check every money request. Acknowledge, bridge and answer, then stop.

checklist: Question 1: What are the six parts of a decision memo? Answer: Decision required, recommendation, why, options considered, risks and next steps.

Question 2: What is Rule 6? Answer: A change to anything that carries load or protects life is approved only in writing, by the person responsible for that design, with the check behind it; a phone call or a stamp without a check is a request, never an approval.

Question 3: You say NOI is about 49 thousand on a call. What is missing, and why does it matter? Answer: The period. If you meant per month and the lender files it as per year, her rough loan sizing is off by a factor of twelve; say both: about 49 thousand a month, about 593 thousand a year.

Question 4: What makes a confirming email useful as a record? Answer: It is sent within a day, numbers each point, states dates, records whether any claim is being made, and sets a deadline for the other side to correct it.

Question 5: A memo asks for 1,500,000 dollars of new equity after cost rises from 10,000,000 to 11,500,000 on a 6,500,000 dollar loan. What does it assume? Answer: That the loan does not increase. If the lender keeps lending 65 percent of cost, the loan rises to 7,475,000 dollars and new equity falls to 525,000 dollars.

Question 6: What are the three steps for a hostile question, and what makes the method honest? Answer: Acknowledge what is true, bridge to what matters, then answer with a fact or a dated commitment. The answer is what makes it honest; without it the method is evasion.
head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned to put decisions on one page and to keep my words reliable. A decision memo has six parts: the decision required with a date, the recommendation, the reasons, the options I rejected, the risks and the next steps. I say every number with its unit and its period, so a monthly figure is never filed as annual and a half-point rate change is never heard as trivial. After any call that decides something, I send a numbered confirming email the same day with a deadline for corrections, and I keep minutes and versions. Rule 6 says a change to anything that carries load or protects life is approved only in writing by the responsible designer with the calculation; the Hyatt Regency collapse is why. I reverse check every money request to find its hidden assumption. And when a question turns hostile, I acknowledge, bridge, answer with a fact or a dated promise, and stop.
terms: Stop-work item — a defect serious enough that the affected work should pause until it is resolved, such as an unapproved structural change.
Funding case — one complete version of how a cost will be paid for, such as with or without a loan increase, shown side by side with another.
One version of the truth — the principle that a project keeps a single, current, agreed record of decisions and documents.

hostile.q: Why did you stop fabrication when the engineer told the contractor the connection was fine?
hostile.a: Because a remark on site is not an approval of a structural change. The engineer of record will review the proposal in writing and return it with calculations. If it is approved, we lose a few days. If it is not, we have avoided building a transfer connection nobody checked. That is a trade I will make every time.
